control.text: Tutorials
Create a page, design its layout, add a Task Set, and publish with eServer.
Jump to the live Task Set walkthrough
See the ProjectAdmin database case study
Follow the database walkthrough
Build a reusable component
Create your first page
1. In ePage Studio, open a project and create a page.
2. Add a panel, set its text and properties, and save the page.
3. Check that the page directory contains page.xml and appears in the project tree.
See the Studio workspace
Build a layout that adapts to the viewport
1. Use a vertical layout for the header and content. Put related controls under one parent in the control tree.
2. Use horizontal docking to keep the content panel aligned with the available width. Use named layers when multiple views share the same area.
3. Preview at a narrow width and check how labels wrap, which areas scroll, and whether buttons are still easy to reach.
Review docking and layout
or
try the view-switching example
Add a click event
1. Select a button or panel on the canvas.
2. Open its onClick event and add a JavaScript handler.
3. Publish and click the control in a browser to verify the result.
sender.style.backgroundColor = "#46368b";
Try a view-switching example
Publish with eServer
1. Register your project directory in the eServer project list.
2. Set the domain and default page where appropriate.
3. Open your public page URL. Test links and image responses in addition to the HTML.
4. For a page with a Task Set, submit a valid request and verify the response. Then test an invalid input and check that the page reports the expected result.
For example, the page directory features in this project is available at /ePage.dev/features.
Build a Task Set that runs on eServer
Use a Task Set when a browser action needs server-side logic. The live form below invokes the named calculateTotal task defined in this page. The multiplication happens inside Script 2 on eServer.
Try the live calculation
Quantity
Unit price in cents
Calculate on eServer
Enter two values and submit to see the result.
See how ProjectAdmin uses Task Set with a database
Set it up in Studio
1. Open the page's Task Set editor and add a named task.
2. Add the three scripts below. The definition is saved as a taskSetItem under taskSet in page.xml.
3. Call calculateTotal() from a browser event. This example calls it from the form's submit handler.
Script 1 ? Prepare in the browser
The form accepts a quantity and a unit price in cents. Write the quantity first and the price second.
Script 2 ? Validate and calculate on eServer
Read the two values in the same order. Check both ranges on the server before multiplying. A zero reply signals rejection because a valid order always has a positive total.
Script 3 ? Display the response in the browser
Read the single integer from the reply and display it in the result area. This is a separate buffer from the two input fields.
Use the same pattern with records or forms
• Load a table. Send the filter, query on eServer, then read the returned data set and populate the table.
• Open a record. Send its ID, check access on eServer, then fill the details controls with the reply.
• Save a form. Send the edited fields, validate and save on eServer, then display the result or reload the list.
If a reply displays incorrectly, compare each writer and reader in sequence. Check the browser request for transport failures and the eServer logs for execution errors.
Task Set in a database application

ProjectAdmin is a separate ePage project for managing tasks and teams. Its main page defines 24 named tasks, including loading a list, creating a task, and editing task information. The screenshot shows the actual getTaskList task in ePage Studio.

control.note: ProjectAdmin Task Sets editor with getTaskList selected and Handle Response Results open. The other tabs are Send Request to Backend and Backend Processing.

control.text: The three tabs correspond to the three scripts. The response checks the status, reads a data set on success, and passes it to the completion callback.
Read a page of results with getTaskList
1. Send Request to Backend. The browser sends the current page index, team selection, and view filter with its session information.
2. Backend Processing. The server checks the session, runs its database queries, and writes a status. On success it follows that status with a data set using eio.appendDataSet.
3. Handle Response Results. The browser clears the busy state and reads the status first. If the response succeeded, it calls eio.readDataSet and hands the rows to the calling code.
Create and update records

taskNewV2 sends form values to eServer to create a task. modifyTaskInfo sends the selected record and edits to update it. Both use db.executeNoneQuery for database writes and return a status string for the browser to handle. A read task can return a data set after its status, while a write task can return a status alone.
Set up a practice database and try the same query and write APIs

When building a similar page, define the request fields and the success and failure replies before editing the scripts. Keep the corresponding reads and writes in the same order, and check access on eServer before querying or changing records.
Connect to a database, then query and edit records
This walkthrough uses a SQL Server practice table and the same eServer database APIs used by ProjectAdmin. Run the SQL and Task Sets against a database created for practice.
1. Register a connection

1. In the ePage project, create a database connection named DemoDb and point its connection string at the practice database. ProjectAdmin stores its named connection under dbConnections in project.xml.

2. Give the practice account access to the table and to the operations you plan to test. Keep the connection string in the server-side project configuration and out of browser scripts and published examples.
3. Create the table and seed it using your database client. Here Status is 0 for open and 1 for complete.
The XML is shown here with a placeholder for the connection string:
<dbConnections count="1"> <connection name="DemoDb"> <connectionString>YOUR_PRACTICE_CONNECTION_STRING</connectionString> </connection> </dbConnections>
In Script 2, db.executeQuery("DemoDb", sql) uses the registered alias. If it returns null, check the alias, eServer's access to the database, the account's permissions, and the SQL in that order.
2. Read rows and return selected columns
Create a Task Set named loadDemoTasks. Call loadDemoTasks() from a browser event. Script 1 can be empty for this fixed query. In Script 2, execute a SELECT and write a status before the data set.

In appendDataSet, the last two arguments are the starting row and the number of rows to return. The explicit column list determines what crosses to the browser. For a single-row lookup, ProjectAdmin uses db.read(result) and a typed getter such as db.getString(result, "columnName").
In Script 3, read the status first. With a table body named taskTable whose columns match the returned fields and a status panel named taskMessage, the response handler can be:
3. Update the row selected in the browser

Create a named write task such as updateDemoTask. In Script 1, read the selected row ID and the new status from controls. Here the form inputs have the IDs task-id and task-status. Require a positive integer ID and a status of 0 or 1 in the form.
eio.appendInt32(Number(document.getElementById("task-id").value)); eio.appendInt32(Number(document.getElementById("task-status").value));
In Script 2, read both integers in the same order and validate them again. In an authenticated application, also verify that the current user may modify that row before executing the statement.

Script 3 reads the one status value with eio.readString8(). On success, call loadDemoTasks() to refresh the list. On failure, keep the edit visible and show a message. A successful statement is distinct from an affected row. If the interface must report a missing or concurrently changed record, use a write operation that reports the affected row count or a database routine that returns that outcome explicitly.
4. Insert and delete practice rows
Use db.executeNoneQuery for commands that do not return a result set. The following separate Script 2 examples use fixed demo values. Run the insert before the delete to test both operations.

For production forms, use a database access path that binds parameters for user-supplied text, and apply authorization before each write. The update example above constructs SQL only from validated integer fields, and the insert and delete use fixed values. Always scope an update or delete to the intended record.
Build a reusable component from a Div

In ePage, a Panel can be the root of a component. Its children make up the interface, custom properties configure each instance, and JavaScript in onCreate implements the behavior. The surrounding page calls the component's methods or reacts to its events.
See the component in a layered application

The Faith desktop main page defines 909 controls and 121 named layers in one page.xml. In Studio, open pc / main and select Explorer to trace the control tree. Start at the main container and follow the central content group (P2) to views such as Home, Search, and Notifications. The menu, side content, secondary views, and dialog overlays have their own groups. A layer groups controls that appear together; a component such as the editor can appear in several of those groups.
1. Start with a Panel and two children

Use one child panel for the label and one for the editable area. On the Home instance, the children have local names c_label and c_edit. In onCreate, resolve children within the instance rather than looking up a page-wide ID. The same internal names can then be used in multiple editors on one page.
2. Create selectable properties and events in Studio
1. Select the component's outer Panel in Explorer. In Properties, select userProperty. The help pane below the grid shows the supported declaration format.

2. Click the … at the right of the userProperty row to open its editor tab. Enter one declaration per line. Return to the UI Editor and use the categorized view of Properties to find the group named in the category field.

3. Select the new property row to choose a value. For a custom event, select its row and click … to open that instance's script editor. The built-in event help displays the handler name and parameters.

control.note: Studio userProperty row and built-in declaration format help

control.text: Select userProperty to see the declaration format in the help pane.

control.note: ProjectAdmin multiSelect property with its true and false choices expanded

control.text: The enum declaration creates an actual dropdown in the Studio property grid.

control.note: ProjectAdmin onComplete event selected with parameter help below the property grid

control.text: The event row shows the handler signature and its parameter help.
The declaration has six fields. Leave a field empty by keeping its separator, such as the empty choices field on editMaxY.
//#P:name|category|defaultValue|type|enumData|help
• name and category. The name becomes the property name, or an event signature with parameters. The category groups rows in Properties.
• defaultValue and enumData. Give an ordinary property a default. For an enum, enter the comma-separated list of choices. The editor example offers compact and comfortable.

• type and help. Studio lists enum, enumFree, string, memo, color, int, double, skin, jsMix, and jsServerEvent. The help text appears when a developer selects the row. The browser-side custom event shown here uses jsMix.

The new editMode example adds a dropdown to the editor pattern. In onCreate, read sender.editMode to choose the spacing and sender.editMaxY to set the height limit. The declaration exposes the setting in Studio, and the component code determines what each choice does.
The screenshots use the ProjectAdmin upload control because it shows both types of editor in one group. These are its property and event declarations with the category and help translated:
//#P:multiSelect|Chunked upload|true|enum|true,false|Allow more than one file //#P:onComplete(sender,worker)|Chunked upload||jsMix||One upload job has finished

Studio opens a separate panel7.onComplete script tab for the event. Likewise, an editor instance can assign a handler to its own onHeightChange row. The component explicitly calls the event after resizing:
For a parent that provides a refresh method, the instance's handler can request a layout refresh:
// In the component instance's onHeightChange event editor: sender.parentNode.refresh();

The original Faith editor declares font family, color, font size, and maximum height. The declarations are stored in userProperty and the selected values and handler bodies are saved under __U_ fields. The Home and mobile composers use a 300px height limit and the posting dialog uses 150px. Each instance can have its own event script.
See multiple files advance in the live upload demo
. It reproduces the uploader's per-file progress and round-robin block scheduling.
3. Implement behavior and expose methods

This simplified onCreate starts with the same two-child structure as the project. It makes the second child editable and exposes methods on sender so the parent can read or replace its text without reaching into the editable child.

The project editor also tracks text, HTML, and caret position. It measures its content height, updates the outer panel, and calls onHeightChange(sender, oldH, newH) when the size changes. Once it reaches its limit, the editable area scrolls.
4. Keep page-specific actions in event handlers
• onInputChange receives the key and before-and-after text and HTML. A handler can return false to cancel an edit.
• onFocusChange reports whether the editable area has focus.
• onCurPosChange receives the old and new caret positions. Faith uses it to check what the user is typing around an @ mention.
• onHeightChange lets the parent reflow the surrounding page. On Home, it refreshes the surrounding composer layout.

Reuse the Panel, its child controls, property declarations, and initialization together. Keep draft text and focus state on the editor instance. A page can send the text to a Task Set when the user submits it.
Try two native advanced editor instances
Try the file upload component

taskSetItem.name: calculateTotal
